{{Short description|Logic-based number-placement puzzle}}
{{about|the puzzle|other uses|Kenken (disambiguation)}}
[[File:Kendoku ans.jpg|thumb|A simple KenKen puzzle, with answers filled in as large numbers.]]
'''KenKen''' and '''KenDoku''' are trademarked names for a style of arithmetic and [[logic puzzle]] invented in 2004 by Japanese math teacher [[Tetsuya Miyamoto]],<ref name="nytimes 2009.feb.08">[https://www.nytimes.com/2009/02/09/arts/09ken.html?_r=1&em A New Puzzle Challenges Math Skills], ''[[New York Times]]'', February 8, 2009</ref> who intended the puzzles to be an instruction-free method of training the brain.<ref name="times 2008.march.21">[https://web.archive.org/web/20080510144756/http://entertainment.timesonline.co.uk/tol/arts_and_entertainment/games_and_puzzles/article3599704.ece Tetsuya Miyamoto creates KenKen. Train your brain], ''[[The Times]]'', 21 March 2008</ref> The name derives from the [[Japanese language|Japanese]] word for {{Nihongo|cleverness|賢|ken, kashiko(i)}}.<ref name="nytimes 2009.feb.08" /> The names '''Calcudoku''' and '''Mathdoku''' are sometimes used by those who do not have the rights to use the KenKen or KenDoku trademarks.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.conceptispuzzles.com/index.aspx?uri=info/news/285|title=KenDoku renamed to CalcuDoku|work=Conceptis Puzzles}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://puzzlemadness.co.uk/faq/|title=Puzzle Madness: Frequently asked questions|publisher=|access-date=2015-04-08|archive-date=2021-01-19|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210119145711/https://puzzlemadness.co.uk/faq|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==General rules==
As in [[Sudoku]], the goal of each puzzle is to fill a grid with digits –– 1 through 4 for a 4×4 grid, 1 through 5 for a 5×5, 1 through 6 for a 6×6, etc. –– so that no digit appears more than once in any row or any column (a [[Latin square]]). Grids range in size from 3×3 to 9×9. Additionally, KenKen grids are divided into heavily outlined groups of cells –– often called “cages” –– and the numbers in the cells of each cage must produce a certain “target” number when combined using a specified mathematical operation (one of addition, [[subtraction]], multiplication or division). For example, a linear three-cell cage specifying addition and a target number of 6 in a 4×4 puzzle must be satisfied with the digits 1, 2, and 3. Digits may be repeated within a cage, as long as they are not in the same row or column. No operation is relevant for a single-cell cage: placing the "target" in the cell is the only possibility (thus being a "free space"). The target number and operation appear in the upper left-hand corner of the cage.

In the English-language KenKen books of [[Will Shortz]], the issue of the non-[[associativity]] of division and subtraction is addressed by restricting clues based on either of those operations to cages of only two cells in which the numbers may appear in any order. Hence if the target is 1 and the operation is - (subtraction) and the number choices are 2 and 3, possible answers are 2,3 or 3,2.   Some puzzle authors have not done this and have published puzzles that use more than two cells for these operations.

==History==
In 2007, toy inventor Robert Fuhrer, owner of Nextoy and creator of [[Gator Golf]], Crocodile Dentist, and dozens of other popular toys and games, encountered KenKen books published in Japan by the educational publisher [[Gakken]] Co., Ltd. and titled  {{nihongo|"Kashikoku naru Puzzle"|賢くなるパズル|Kashikoku naru pazuru|lit. "to become smart puzzle"}}.<ref name="times 2008.march.21"/>  Fuhrer's company [[Nextoy]], [[Limited liability company|LLC]] (now holder of a trademark on "KenKen" and "KenDoku" as a name for brain-training puzzles) and chess International Master [[David Levy (chess player)|David Levy]] helped bring the puzzles to the attention of Michael Harvey, an editor of ''[[The Times]]'' (London).<ref name="The Next Sudoku?">Stephey, M. J. [https://web.archive.org/web/20090316093406/http://www.time.com/time/magazine/article/0,9171,1884862,00.html "The Next Sudoku?"] Time Magazine 23 Mar. 2009: 72.</ref> Harvey, impressed with what he calls its "depth and magnitude", arranged for publication of such puzzles, starting in March 2008, in ''The Times''. Other papers, including the ''[[New York Times]]'', followed suit. KenKen now appears in more than 200 newspapers in the [[United States]] and worldwide. In 2014, KenKen signed an agreement with DTI, the software division of inflight entertainment expert Advanced Flight Alliance AG, and its parent company Global Eagle Entertainment, to provide KenKen on international flights.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://airfax.com/blog/index.php/2014/02/11/dti-to-bring-popular-brain-game-kenken-to-inflight-entertainment/|title = DTI to Bring Popular Brain Game "KenKen®" to Inflight Entertainment : IFExpress}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.prweb.com/releases/kenken_puzzles_take_to_the_skies/prweb11572980.htm|title=KenKen Puzzles Take to the Skies|date=17 February 2014|work=PRWeb}}</ref>  In 2015, KenKen partnered with German news organization ''[[Der Spiegel]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.spiegel.de/wissenschaft/mensch/kenken-kostenlos-online-spielen-a-994418.html|title=Kenken kostenlos online spielen|author=((SPIEGEL ONLINE, Hamburg, Germany))|date=2 December 2014|work=SPIEGEL ONLINE}}</ref> The magazine, which is one of Europe's largest news publications, offers KenKen puzzles on their mobile app.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.spiegel.de/wissenschaft/mensch/kenken-app-fuer-android-und-ios-kostenlos-a-1041247.html|title=KenKen-App für Android und iOS - kostenlos|author=((SPIEGEL ONLINE, Hamburg, Germany))|date=1 July 2015|work=SPIEGEL ONLINE}}</ref> KenKen is also being used by over 30,000 teachers throughout the United States to teach math skills, [[problem solving]] techniques, logic, and [[critical thinking]].<ref>Kulkarni, D. [http://www.matholympiad.info/Documents/TeachingWithKenKen.pdf Enjoying Math: Learning Problem Solving With KenKen Puzzles] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130801080339/http://www.matholympiad.info/Documents/TeachingWithKenKen.pdf |date=2013-08-01 }},  A textbook for teaching with KenKen Puzzles.</ref> Today KenKen can be played online at [http://www.kenkenpuzzle.com www.kenkenpuzzle.com], as well as on its iOS, [[Android (operating system)|Android]] and Kindle Fire apps.

==Example==
[[Image:KenKenProblem.svg|right|300px|thumb| A typical KenKen problem.]]
[[Image:KenKenSolution.svg|right|300px|thumb| Solution to the above problem.]]
The objective is to fill the grid in with the digits 1 through 6 so that:
* Each row contains exactly one of each digit
* Each column contains exactly one of each digit
* Each bold-outlined group of cells is a cage containing digits which achieve the specified result using the specified mathematical operation: addition (+), subtraction (−), multiplication (×), and division (÷). (Unlike [[Killer Sudoku]], digits may repeat within a cage.)

Some of the techniques from Sudoku and Killer Sudoku can be used here, but much of the process involves the listing of all the possible options and eliminating the options one by one as other information requires.

In the example here:
: (sets of numbers such as "5,6" and "4,5" could appear in any order)
* "11+" in the leftmost column can only be "5,6"
* "2÷" in the top row must be one of "1,2", "2,4" or "3,6"
* "20×" in the fourth column must be "4,5".
* "6×" in the top right must be "1,1,2,3". Therefore, the two "1"s must be in separate columns, thus row 1 column 5 is a "1".
* "30x" in the fourth row down must contain "5,6"
* "240×" on the left side is one of "6,5,4,2" or "3,5,4,4". Either way the five must be in the upper right cell because we have "5,6" already in column 1, and "5,6" in row 4. Also, then the combination must be "3,5,4,4" because there is nowhere to put the 6, with the above criteria.

==Extensions==
More complex KenKen problems are formed using the principles described above but omitting the symbols +, −, × and ÷, thus leaving them as yet another unknown to be determined.  Other authors of puzzles include more complex operations, including exponentiation, modulus, and bit-wise operations.  Ranges of values can be varied, such as including zero, or having negative values (e.g., -2 to +2 in a 5-by-5 square).

==Education==
One of KenKen's main uses is in the classroom as a means of teaching basic arithmetic and logic skills. In 2009, KenKen LLC began the KenKen Classroom (KKCR) Program, which allowed teachers to subscribe to a weekly newsletter providing KenKen puzzle sets, as well as other brain teasers, and KenKen news. Today, over 25,000 educators are a part of the KKCR Program. In addition to KKCR, KenKen also helps educators organize their own KenKen clubs and tournaments in their schools. KenKen partners with educators to help students learn while having fun. KenKen has collaborated with the [[National Council of Teachers of Mathematics]] (NCTM), to create a mobile app in order to help students develop their math and logic skills.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nctm.org/Publications/mathematics-teacher/2013/Vol107/Issue5/Using-KenKen-to-Build-Reasoning-Skills/|title=Using KenKen to Build Reasoning Skills|publisher=}}</ref>  KenKen is featured on [[Scholastic Corporation]]'s online sites Scholastic Math and Scholastic Dynamath,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://teacher.scholastic.com/scholasticnews/magazines/assets/mathkenken.htm|title=Today's KenKen Puzzles|publisher=}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://teacher.scholastic.com/scholasticnews/magazines/assets/dynakenken.htm|title=Today's KenKen Puzzles|publisher=}}</ref> as well as on The Math Forum @ Drexel.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://mathforum.org/kenken/|title=KenKen @ The Math Forum|publisher=}}</ref>

==Tournaments==
Beginning in 2010, KenKen CEO Robert Fuhrer has organized yearly KenKen tournaments held at the Chappaqua Library in [[Chappaqua, New York]]. Tournaments are open to all ages and skill levels. In addition to the Chappaqua tournament in December, Fuhrer partnered with IBM to host an international tournament in May 2015. In 2016, five students in India, Gaurav Pandey, Neharika Rajesh, Visharad Srivastava, Devika Pillai and Kajal Agarwal, beat 75,000 competitors to secure a place in the International Round that was held in New York on 18th Dec 2016. In addition to the visitors, many local students ages 8–18 competed in the tournament. The tournament was won by eight-year-old Gaurav Pandey, who beat out competitors up to twice his age.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.indiatoday.in/world/story/kenken-international-puzzle-championship-indian-students-outshine-256483-2015-06-09|title=Indian students outshine at KenKen International Puzzle Championship|date=9 June 2015 |publisher=}}</ref> In 2016, the United Arab Emirates also took part in KenKen International Championship, with over 6000 students from more than 60 schools participating. Of those, eight of the top ranking students from the UAE 2016 finals represented the country in the International Level round in [[New York City]] on December 18:<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.khaleejtimes.com/nation/dubai/kenken-is-the-new-sudoku-for-young-minds-in-uae|title=UAE to host KenKen International Puzzle Championship for first time|publisher=Khaleej Times}}</ref> Eeshan Sharma from GEMS Modern Academy; Ganesh Ramm from The Oxford School, Dubai; Helem Jos from Sunrise English Private School; Mythri Muralikannan from The Millennium School Dubai; Paarth Gupta from GEMS Dubai American Academy; Aryaman Chawla from Dubai College; Gamin Kwon from The English College; and Ghaia Aljarwan from Rosary School.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.educationjournalme.com/news/eight-uae-students-to-compete-in-kenken-global-finals-in-december_111363|title=Eight UAE students to compete in Kenken global finals in December|publisher=Education Journal}}</ref>

In December 2016, the KenKen International Championship was held in New York City. Winners were John Gilling, Ellie Grueskin and Molly Olonoff.
<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.kenkenchampionship.com/past-tournament|title=KenKen International Championship Winners}}</ref> In December 2017, the KenKen International Championship was held in Pleasantville, N.Y. Winners were John Gilling, Ellie Grueskin and Mike Holman.
<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theexaminernews.com/puzzles-and-ping-pong-collide-at-kenken-tourney-in-pleasantville/|title=Puzzles and PingPong Collide at KenKen Tourney|date=18 December 2017}}</ref>

Over the past several years KenKen has expanded internationally and now runs national tournaments in multiple countries for students. There are three age groups and the student winners of each division attend the KenKen International Championship in New York.  Student divisions include Sigma (Approximate age is 14 and up), Kappa (Approximate age 11–14), and Delta (Approximate age 11 and younger). There is also an adult division and a senior division for those over the age of 60.
